goal: A merge conflict is resolved where it is cheapest: by git for the files whose resolution is mechanical, by the runner for its own plan format, and — only for what is left — by the step session that had to read the code anyway.
`reconcile` stops being a session kind. No round pays a cold session to finish a merge and then stop.
contract: Martin ruled all three layers on 2026-09-04, against the measurement below: `reconcile` goes.
A step session that meets a conflict resolves it and then does its step, in the same session. It never lands the merge and stops.

No conflict is resolved by weakening the result. `merge=union` is only for a file whose two sides append and never edit the same line; a plan is merged by the rule that already says who may write what, not by taking a side.

The memoro half — memoro's own `.gitattributes` and getting `sdk:check` into its gate — is `docs/project/test-architecture/generated-artifact-merge/PLAN.json` in memoro. Neither plan waits for the other, and this one changes no file in memoro.
out_of_scope: memoro's `.gitattributes`, and `scripts/testing/ci.mjs`. A step here has a memoro-cli workarea and cannot reach them: `repoOf` (`src/mc/run.js`) returns the repository whose checkout the workarea holds.
The `repair` kind, and everything in `~/mc/runner/held.json`. A held pull request is a different mechanism with a different cause.

`replayOnto` and the stacked-branch retarget. Its comment says a conflict there is *not* what reconcile is for, and it stays that way — this project does not change what happens when a squashed base breaks the branch above it.
Whether the runner merges or rebases `origin/main` into a project branch. `syncMain` merges and never rebases; that is not revisited here.

The three `reconcile*` names that mean something else: `reconcileHeld` (`src/mc/held.js:157`) and `reconcileHold` (`src/mc/run.js:442`) are about held pull requests, not merges. Nothing in this project touches them.

success_criteria.criterion: Two branches that each append a row to the project log merge without a conflict, keeping both rows.
success_criteria.check: In a scratch clone: branch A appends a row, branch B a different one, `git merge` succeeds, `tail` shows both. Output pasted in the PR.

success_criteria.criterion: A `PLAN.json` conflict where the two sides changed different steps is resolved by the runner with no session.
success_criteria.check: A test builds the three stages of such a conflict, runs the resolver, and asserts the result carries both sides' changes and passes `validatePlan`. A conflict the rule cannot resolve is left in progress, asserted separately.

success_criteria.criterion: A step session handed a conflicted worktree resolves it and delivers its step in the same session.
success_criteria.check: Seen in `~/mc/runner/log/runs.tsv`: a row whose project had a conflict that round, `kind` `step`, ending `success,merged` or with a pull request. Not asserted from the code.
`grep -rn 'reconcile' src/ canon/ docs/technical/` returns only `reconcileHeld` and `reconcileHold`. `chooseKind` has no branch that returns it.

success_criteria.criterion: The runner still stops rather than guessing when a conflict is not resolvable.
success_criteria.check: A test drives a round whose conflict neither git nor the plan rule can resolve, and asserts the project is skipped with the conflicting files named — never a session launched on a half-merged tree with no instructions about it.

steps.title: The project log stops conflicting
steps.done_when: Two branches that each append a row to `docs/project/project_log.md` merge cleanly and keep both rows.
instruction: memoro-cli has no `.gitattributes` at all. Create one with `docs/project/project_log.md merge=union`, and nothing else — every other conflict measured in this repository was real content.

`union` is a built-in git driver and needs no `git config`, unlike the `generated` driver memoro installs from `scripts/setup-hooks.sh`. That matters here: `mc run` merges inside worktrees it creates itself (`syncMain`, `src/mc/run.js`), and a driver that has to be installed per clone would not be in force where the conflicts happen.

Write the limit into the comment beside the line. `union` keeps both sides of every conflicting hunk, which is right for a table only ever appended to and wrong the moment a row is edited or reordered — the result is a duplicated row nobody notices. This is a claim about how the close-out row is written, not a general policy, and the next person adding a line to this file needs to read that before they do.
Verify it. Scratch clone, two branches each appending a distinct row, `git merge`, read the tail, paste it in the PR. `git check-attr merge -- docs/project/project_log.md` says `union`.
comments: The repository now has a `.gitattributes` at its root, and it holds one rule: `docs/project/project_log.md merge=union`. Step 4 adds the close-out row to that file, so its merge against a `main` that gained rows meanwhile is now git's problem and not a session's — but only for an appended row. The comment block above the line says why, and step 4 should not edit or reorder an existing row without reading it first.

The counterfactual was measured, not assumed: with the driver removed and nothing else changed, the same two branches conflict (`CONFLICT (content)`, one marker set). So the clean merge is the attribute doing the work, not the two rows happening to land apart.

`union` is in force inside `mc run`'s own worktrees without any setup, because git reads `.gitattributes` from the merge's working tree and `union` is built in. That is the reason the driver is `union` and not memoro's installed `generated` driver, which `scripts/setup-hooks.sh` has to configure per clone and which therefore would not be in force where `syncMain` merges.

steps.title: A plan conflict is resolved by the plan's own rule
steps.done_when: A `PLAN.json` conflict whose two sides changed different steps is resolved by the runner without a session, and one that breaks the rule is left in progress.
instruction: 29 of the 166 conflicting files measured in `~/mc/runner/log/runner.log` were `PLAN.json` or `PLAN.md`. The shape is always the same: main carries a plan a later round wrote to, the branch carries the same plan with its own step edited. That is exactly the comparison the runner already knows how to make — `unauthorisedChanges(before, after, index)` in `src/mc/plan-schema.js` says which fields belong to whom: everything outside `steps[index]` and `met` is not the session's.

Run it as a merge rather than as a check. During a conflicted merge git holds all three sides in the index: `git show :1:<path>` is the merge base, `:2:` is ours, `:3:` is theirs. Parse all three as JSON, and build the result field by field — for each step, take whichever side changed it against the base; for `met`, take a criterion as met if either side met it; for `goal`, `contract`, `out_of_scope` and the criteria themselves, take main's, because a step session may not have changed them and the planning session's edit is the one on main.

Refuse rather than guess. If both sides changed the same step, or either side does not parse as JSON, or the result fails `validatePlan`, this file is not resolved — leave it conflicted and let the round fall through to the next step's path. A resolver that guesses on a plan produces a plan the next session acts on without checking, which is the most expensive kind of wrong in this system.

Where it goes: `syncMain` (`src/mc/run.js`) already has one special case of this shape — an identical `.gitignore` hunk, resolved inline with `checkout --theirs` and a commit. This is the second, and it is bigger than an inline branch; put the rule in its own module beside `plan-schema.js` so it can be tested without a git repository, and call it from `syncMain` with the conflicted paths.

Test the rule, not the plumbing: build the three stages as objects, assert the merged result carries both sides' changes and passes `validatePlan`, and assert each refusal case returns no result. Then `npm test`.
comments: The rule is `src/mc/plan-merge.js`: `mergePlans({ base, branch, main })` over three parsed plans, `mergePlanText` over the three texts, and `isPlanPath` for the conflicted path. The three sides are named rather than ordered on purpose — `branch` is ours and `main` is theirs, and getting them the wrong way round would hand the branch's step edits to main's authority and silently lose them. The frozen field list is now `PLAN_FROZEN_FIELDS` in `plan-schema.js`, read by both `unauthorisedChanges` and the merge, so the check and the merge cannot drift apart.

Step 3 changes `syncMain`'s caller, not `syncMain` itself. What is there now: every conflicted path that `isPlanPath` recognises goes through `resolvePlanConflict`, which reads `:1:`/`:2:`/`:3:` with `git show`, writes the merged file, and stages it; when nothing is left conflicted the runner commits the merge itself. Files the rule refuses stay conflicted and are returned in `sync.conflicts` — so `sync.conflicts` is now what is *left*, which is exactly the list step 3 wants to name in the step session's preamble. One case worth knowing: everything resolved but `git commit` refusing returns `{ ok: false, conflicts: [] }`, which the round already treats as a skip, so no session starts in a worktree mid-merge.

A resolved plan is re-serialised (`JSON.stringify(plan, null, 2)`), not patched, so the merge commit carries a canonically formatted file whatever the two sides looked like. That is safe because nothing reads a plan as text — the trespass check, the page and the runner all parse it — but it does mean the merge commit's diff of a hand-formatted plan can be wide.

Measured against real git, not only against the fixture: in a scratch repo, two branches editing different steps of the same `PLAN.json` conflict, `git show :1:/:2:/:3:` returns base/ours/theirs as assumed, and writing `mergePlanText`'s output plus `git add` plus `git commit --no-edit` completes the merge with no `MERGE_HEAD` left and both sides' changes in the file.

steps.title: The step session takes the conflict
steps.done_when: A round that meets a conflict git and the plan rule could not resolve launches a `step` session on the conflicted worktree, and that session resolves it and delivers its step.
instruction: Today the round reads `const plan = sync.conflicts.length ? null : planOf(worktree, name)` (`src/mc/run.js`), so a conflict makes the plan unreadable to the runner by construction and `chooseKind` (`src/mc/run-plan.js`) returns `{ kind: 'reconcile' }` before it looks at anything else. Both halves change: the plan is still read, and the conflict is something the step session is told about rather than a different kind of session.

Read the plan from `HEAD` while a merge is in progress. The file in the worktree may itself carry conflict markers — after step 2 that is rarer, but a plan whose two sides changed the same step is exactly the case step 2 refuses. `git show HEAD:<plan path>` is the branch's own last good copy, and it is the right one: the step the session is being handed is the step this branch is on.

`stepPrompt` gains a conflict preamble when there is one — the files by name, that a `git merge origin/main` is in progress and stopped on them, and that resolving it is the first thing to do and not the whole job. Keep the existing body after it unchanged; the session's step, its `done_when` and what it may write in the plan are all still true.

The resolution rules that `canon/roles/reconcile.md` carried are the part worth keeping, and they move to the step role: keep this branch's intent and main's changes both; a generated file (SDK artifacts, corpora, manifests, inventories) is regenerated with the repository's own script, found in `package.json` or the docs, never hand-edited; after a keep-both resolution, check no hunk was kept twice. Where that text goes depends on what has landed: `role-instructions` (this programme, in parallel) introduces a shared entry every role inherits. If it has landed, put what is common there and the rest in `step.md`; if it has not, put all of it in `canon/roles/step.md` plainly and say so in the PR. Do not wait for it and do not reshape the catalogue here.

Keep the failure path as clear as the one it replaces. Today a merge that the session does not finish is aborted (`if (kind === 'reconcile' && ... MERGE_HEAD ...) git merge --abort`), which leaves the worktree clean for the next round. A step session that cannot resolve the conflict must land in a state as clean: decide whether the abort still runs for a step session that left `MERGE_HEAD` behind, and say why in the PR. A half-merged worktree carried into the next round is the one outcome worse than today's cold session.

`npm test`, and then watch one real round: the criterion for this step is a row in `~/mc/runner/log/runs.tsv` with `kind` `step` for a project that had a conflict that round. Read `runner.log` for the `merge conflict in:` line that names it.

steps.title: Remove the kind, and close out
steps.done_when: `grep -rn 'reconcile' src/ canon/ docs/technical/` returns only `reconcileHeld` and `reconcileHold`, and `docs/project/project_log.md` has the row.
instruction: What goes: `canon/roles/reconcile.md`, `reconcilePrompt` (`src/mc/run-plan.js`), the branch in `chooseKind` that returns the kind, the `MERGE_HEAD` abort keyed on it (`src/mc/run.js`) unless step 3 kept it for step sessions, its arm of the merged/ran verdict (`kind === 'reconcile' && note === 'success'`), and the colour in `src/mc/page-render.js`.

What must not go, and it reads identically to a grep: `reconcileHeld` (`src/mc/held.js:157`) and `reconcileHold` (`src/mc/run.js:442`) are about reconciling `~/mc/runner/held.json` against the open pull requests. Different mechanism, different word, and nothing in this project touches them.

`runs.tsv` keeps its history. 64 rows carry `reconcile` as their `kind` and they are the measurement this project was planned on; nothing rewrites them, and whatever reads that column tolerates a value it no longer produces. Check `src/mc/brief-collect.js`'s run summary and `src/mc/page-collect.js` before assuming they do.

The documentation: `docs/technical/mc-run.md` describes the kind in four places (the kinds table, the sync section, what the roles are, and the workarea section) and `docs/technical/mc-ui.md` in two (the colour table and the shared vocabulary). Replace them with what now happens — git resolves, the runner resolves a plan, the step session resolves the rest — rather than deleting the paragraphs and leaving a gap where a reader expects the answer.

Add the row to `docs/project/project_log.md`, naming the memoro half (`generated-artifact-merge`) so a reader of either log finds the other. In the PR, give the count: of the 67 conflict events measured, how many the three layers now take without a session, on the same categorisation the plan was sized against — 37 were entirely mechanical, 13 mixed, 17 real code.
